articles.text: Alyssa Dykman hits the ground running as Piedmont’s first Sustainability Program Manager In its continuing movement to live by its own words, the City of Piedmont hired Alyssa Dykman on November 30 as its first Sustainability Program Manager. She is already reeling from a major achievement – the city’s approval of reach codes on February 1, a goal she helped achieve with extensive community outreach. As the community continues to make strides toward its ambitious Climate Action Plan, she will be tasked with leading the citywide programs and activities that advance its efforts. The Climate Action Plan is meant to be a roadmap for residents that outlines collective and individual actions to combat the climate crisis. Piedmont’s goals are especially ambitious: to reduce greenhouse gas (GHG) emissions 40 percent by 2030 and 80 percent by 2050. The creation of Dykman’s new title comes from the city’s long-standing support for sustainability issues, including Piedmont Connect, an organization that supports citizen initiatives and city efforts to build a more sustainable future. “One of the top priorities from the city’s Climate Action Plan was to invest more in staff’s capacity to pursue sustainability, and the creation of this position reflects just that,” Dykman said. Many responsibilities fit under this new title. Dykman will oversee programs and activities that pertain to environmental management and sustainability, including Alyssa Dykman the areas of climate action, clean water and solid waste collection and diversion, recycling, and more. She also serves as a liaison for external, technical, and advisory groups in these areas at the local and regional level. In Piedmont she works with all city departments to establish procedures and ensure compliance with sustainable practices. The position requires wearing a number of hats, Dykman admitted, including having a comfortable command of public engagement and education initiatives. Immediately after being hired, Dykman had to hit the ground running. She joined the city staff after the first reading of reach codes. A wide variety of concerns were brought up by both city councilmembers and residents on July 20, 2020, and a second reading was deferred until more public outreach could be conducted. “I understood coming in that reach codes were an immediate priority, but that it required “Dude recommends that we establish a better balance between the Work ethic and the Martini ethic.”

articles.text: Reupholstering firm is celebrating its 100th anniversary this year Kay Chesterfield, Inc. is a furniture reupholstery business with deep Piedmont roots. Like so many businesses, they are fighting to survive the coronavirus pandemic. The market for reupholstering furniture has swayed dramatically. Businesses no longer prioritize the furnishing of indoor spaces since there are limited indoor customers. To stay in business, owner Kriss Kokoefer had to adapt their work to focus on residential clients. Kokoefer bought the company in 2013 from long-time owners and Piedmont residents John and Jo Anne Jones. Kay Chesterfield, Inc. is celebrating its 100th birthday this year. Some reupholstery businesses have seen a boom in business during the pandemic, leading to long wait times of multiple months. Kay Chesterfield differs from other reupholstery business as their primary income has been from commercial clients. Without that business their lead time is down to three or four weeks once the furniture and fabrics come in. “Our commercial business is down, which makes sense because people are not in the office right now. Another big part of our business comes from hospitality and hotels, and they are pretty much hurting now, too,” Kokoefer said. Kay Chesterfield’s biggest customer has been San Francisco airport, but with travel drastically reduced, so goes Kay Chesterfield. With a smile, Kokoefer continued. “The flipside is residential sales are going crazy. People are home, and they have time to actually do home projects. Many people are sitting at home and just staring at their furniture,” she explained. Kokoefer’s business is a big operation, with 16 employees. Most upholsters work out of their garage or a small storefront and maybe have one or two employees. The Chesterfield firm is unique in that it is large enough to have project managers. Customers receive a lot of hand-holding to ensure they get exactly what they want. “Residential is not sustaining our business, however. The PPP loan helped, but we need to Kriss Kokoefer, owner of Kay Chesterfield Upholstering, stands under the iconic Kay Chesterfield sign across from the Oakland Coliseum. crawl out of the hole,” Kokoefer explained. Kokoefer started off in the industry by selling furniture but then got interested in the impact upon human health when furniture is thrown away. Furniture disposal and cleaning furniture involves toxic materials. Revamping existing chairs, couches and tables has a big impact on the health of the environment. Kay Chesterfield launched a website in January (www. kaychesterfield.com) with a shiny new slogan that sounds more like the Army: “Re-Up.” But it hits the mark on reminding businesses and individuals to focus on why reupholstering furniture is sustainable, while explaining the environmental impacts of disposing of the old pieces. Furniture waste is substantial, 9.8 million tons of furniture goes to landfills per year in the U.S. alone. Each year around two tons of old furniture pieces end up getting burned at U.S. waste sites. Two large sectional sofas produce 1.5 tons of CO2 when burned, which is equivalent to a car driving 4,000 miles. Kokoefer pointed out popular trends taking place in the world of redoing home furnishing. “People are taking something that looks like a wing chair or an antique chair and putting on modern fabric. The juxtaposition of old and new highlights that you were able to create something unique that nobody else has,” Kokoefer explained. Wools have become the en vogue fabric according to Kokoefer. Wools are inherently antimicrobial, stain resistant, and easily cleaned. Also, they have no added toxins and are biodegradable. Kay Chesterfield is located at 6365 Coliseum Way in Oakland. articles.text: The Mars Perseverance rover will land on the red planet on Thursday, February 18 at 12:30 p.m. after a seven-month, 300-million-mile journey. Chabot Space & Science Center will celebrate the landing of NASA’s Mars Perseverance rover with a virtual watch party tomorrow, Thursday, February 18 from 12:00 to 2:00 p.m. During this historic, virtual event, guests are invited to witness the landing with Chabot astronomers and NASA experts who worked on the mission. Tune in to see the landing live on Facebook and YouTube with Chabot’s watch party at chabotspace.org/calendar/nasamars-perseverance-rover-landing-watch-party/. The Perseverance rover will make history when it touches down on the red planet at 12:30 p.m. PST. Before landing, the rover must face the “seven minutes of terror,” a complex and critical landing phase with a series of specific maneuvers. Chabot astronomers will answer questions throughout the landing and make live observations. After the landing, learn more about the mission at a virtual Q&A session with NASA scientists at 1 p.m. NASA’s Ames Research Center engineers Shanna Withrow-Maser and Winnie Kuang will discuss their roles in Mars exploration and answer questions from the public. To celebrate the rover landing, Chabot Space & Science Center is providing a variety of free Mars-themed activities, virtual events and teacher resources.
articles.title: Chabot Space & Science Center hosts watch party for Mars rover landing

articles.text: Distance learning presents impediments to all students, and for some, learning exclusively on a computer can seem all but impossible. For decades, educators at all levels have attempted to diversify how lessons are taught to account for the different ways in which students learn best. Unfortunately, with every lesson on a screen, education has become one dimensional (or 2-D at best). There’s really no substitute for on-campus, in-class learning. But until then, try getting the leftbrain involved. For students considered solitary, auditory, mathematic or visual learners, screen-based learning may be okay. Roughly 25 percent pf Piedmont families with elementary school age students have chosen to continue with distance learning. While many factors went into those decisions, it is fair to say that distance learning is tolerable for some students. Students who learn most efficiently from social, verbal and physical teaching may be struggling the most with distance learning. Using color, making artistic representations, utilizing alternative school supplies and employing music can awaken the left brain often forgotten in education. Piedmont kindergarteners went back to in-person learning last week on February 10. Much insight can actually be gleaned from the youngest learners to help older students. The joy of learning has vanished for many. An overarching goal for a tutor, beyond re-explaining course material, is to inspire passion and make education fun. Something as simple as using different color pens, or pencils can make note-taking easier and more enjoyable. In college I adopted the habit of going over my notes right after a lecture or discussion and adding comments in a different color. When looking at the notes later, Give your computer a rest and use a typewriter, like this 1920’s Corona machine. It’s fun, auditory and a tactile way to hammer out schoolwork. I would use another color. This keeps a record of how thoughts develop. Drawing picture representations in the margin of notes can really solidify material too. Having a fancy set of color pencils can make all the difference. It can be tricky to get the left brain involved in a subject like math, but it’s not impossible. Again, investing in school supplies can make all the difference. While often shunned and forgotten as archaic, writing with quill and ink, or using a vintage typewriter can bring excitement to the most droll of subjects. While cursive handwriting has been phased out of grade school education, for some, the graceful font can be just enough artistic activity to keep sentences flowing. Enliven the left brain When pre-schoolers, students, or professionals, are totally swept up in a project and just going for it, productivity is at a maximum. Often that occurs when both sides of the brain are engaged. It doesn’t take a CT scan to notice that people are the most entrenched in their tasks when creativity and the whole brain are unleashed. Music in the background can help set the right mood for studying. Classical music and jazz have a mellow cadence and the songs are long, which encourage long periods of unbroken attention without too much change. For more contemporary music fans, instrumental beats, or electronic music can accomplish the same thing. Try lowering the volume or listening to music without lyrics if tunes with vocals are distracting. Students who are musicians may want to try turning course material into songs or simply reading out loud while adding a cadence to it. Student isolation lends itself to singing out loud, even during class (just make sure the microphone is muted). Taking this principle to the next level, a student could employ a younger sibling to translate course material into a play or into a stand-up routine. Type up a script and get theatrical. It can be fun and memorable. Whether studying, doing homework or merely trying to stay awake during class, using unique study methods can give students a little edge – and a boost of confidence. Jay Russel has over 10 years of experience as a tutor; he specializes in essay writing and algebra.
articles.title: ADVICE FROM A TUTOR: Use the left brain

Using color, making artistic representations, utilizing alternative school supplies and employing music can awaken the left brain often forgotten in education. Piedmont kindergarteners went back to in-person learning last week on February 10. Much insight can actually be gleaned from the youngest learners to help older students. The joy of learning has vanished for many. An overarching goal for a tutor, beyond re-explaining course material, is to inspire passion and make education fun. Something as simple as using different color pens, or pencils can make note-taking easier and more enjoyable. In college I adopted the habit of going over my notes right after a lecture or discussion and adding comments in a different color. When looking at the notes later, Give your computer a rest and use a typewriter, like this 1920’s Corona machine. It’s fun, auditory and a tactile way to hammer out schoolwork. I would use another color. This keeps a record of how thoughts develop. Drawing picture representations in the margin of notes can really solidify material too. Having a fancy set of color pencils can make all the difference. It can be tricky to get the left brain involved in a subject like math, but it’s not impossible. Again, investing in school supplies can make all the difference. While often shunned and forgotten as archaic, writing with quill and ink, or using a vintage typewriter can bring excitement to the most droll of subjects. While cursive handwriting has been phased out of grade school education, for some, the graceful font can be just enough artistic activity to keep sentences flowing. Enliven the left brain When pre-schoolers, students, or professionals, are totally swept up in a project and just going for it, productivity is at a maximum. Often that occurs when both sides of the brain are engaged. It doesn’t take a CT scan to notice that people are the most entrenched in their tasks when creativity and the whole brain are unleashed. Music in the background can help set the right mood for studying. Classical music and jazz have a mellow cadence and the songs are long, which encourage long periods of unbroken attention without too much change. For more contemporary music fans, instrumental beats, or electronic music can accomplish the same thing. Try lowering the volume or listening to music without lyrics if tunes with vocals are distracting. Students who are musicians may want to try turning course material into songs or simply reading out loud while adding a cadence to it. Student isolation lends itself to singing out loud, even during class (just make sure the microphone is muted). Taking this principle to the next level, a student could employ a younger sibling to translate course material into a play or into a stand-up routine. Type up a script and get theatrical. It can be fun and memorable. Whether studying, doing homework or merely trying to stay awake during class, using unique study methods can give students a little edge – and a boost of confidence. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. articles.text: Appointments are now available for eligible Alameda County residents for COVID-19 vaccinations at the Oakland-Alameda County Coliseum. This is the first federally operated vaccination “supersite” in the country. The vaccination site opened yesterday, February 16, and is jointly operated by the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) and the State of California through the Governor’s Office of Emergency Services (Cal OES). In addition, a mass vaccination site was established at California State University, Los Angeles, as part of Gov. Newsom’s pilot project as part of the wider effort to establish 100 vaccination sites nationwide in the federal administration’s first 100 days. “In the fight against COVID- 19, partnership is key, especially when it comes to reaching Californians in underserved areas,” said Newsom. “These new sites will help us get available supply to some of the California communities most in need. I thank the Biden Administration for standing with us as we continue our efforts to safely, swiftly and equitably vaccinate all Californians.” FEMA is providing resources and federal staffing support to establish these new community vaccination centers, as well as operational support. The Oakland Coliseum mass vaccination site will eventually have the capacity Health professionals at the Oakland Coliseum are now prepared to administer COVID-19 vaccinations to eligible Alameda County residents, beginning February 16. to administer up to 6,000 vaccine doses per day. The two locations chosen for these efforts, Los Angeles and Alameda County, are communities that have been disproportionately impacted by COVID-19 and are home to essential workers who have “borne the brunt of keeping the economy open over the past year,” Newsom said. “This additional resource and infusion of vaccine is much needed in our community and will help us to reach more people more quickly,” Colleen Chawla, Director of the Alameda County Health Care Services Agency (HCSA), said. “We look forward to working with the site team to support outreach, education and access for our highest risk communities.” Alameda County Health Director Nicolas Moss advised that precautionary measures should still be taken, even after receiving the vaccine. “While we work to vaccinate County residents, we urge everyone to continue the other measures proven to slow the spread of COVID-19, including wearing masks and practicing physical distancing,” Moss said. “These simple strategies are the best way for people to remain safe and to protect their loved ones and co-workers until more people are vaccinated.” You can sign up for an appointment by visiting https://myturn. ca.gov/. Everyone in California will have an opportunity to get vaccinated to prevent COVID-19 at no cost. At this time, the state is beginning to vaccinate those at highest risk, such as individuals with a high risk of exposure and people ages 65 and older. To find out if you are eligible at this time, click on https:// myturn.ca.gov/.

articles.text: Congresswoman Barbara Lee of Oakland announced on February 10 that $2 billion in Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) funds would be used to allow families to afford proper funerals for loved ones who have died as a result of COVID-19. The program will allow families to be reimbursed up to $7,000 for funeral expenses and will be retroactive through the beginning of the pandemic (January 2020) to December 31, 2020. It replicates the funding used for funeral assistance in the aftermath of Hurricane Katrina and was inspired by legislation introduced by Congresswoman Lee and Congresswoman Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez (NY-14) in May 2020. “This must be a top priority in our response to this crisis. I’m proud to have partnered with Congresswoman Ocasio-Cortez and Senator Schumer on this crucial relief measure for families in California and across the country already beset by unimaginable grief,” Lee said. Ocasio-Cortez’s bill directs FEMA to provide financial assistance to individuals and funeral homes for the funeral expenses of an individual who died of COVID-19 without sufficient insurance to pay for such Rep. Barbara Lee expenses. The bill also limits assistance for funeral expenses to $10,000 for each deceased individual and prohibits FEMA from requiring residence in a presidentially declared disaster area as a condition for receiving assistance. “No one should struggle to afford a proper funeral for a loved one. During this time of unprecedented pain and economic hardship, it’s a moral imperative that the federal government step in and provide relief,” Lee said. “FEMA is authorized for $2 billion as of right now and it is retroactive, reimbursing back to January 2020. Those interested in participating in the program will need expense documentation, a death certificate, and other personal information documents.”
articles.title: Rep. Barbara Lee announces federal funding for COVID-19 funeral expenses

The Alameda County Public Health Department reported that 2,365 Piedmonters have received their first dose of the vaccine, representing roughly 21 percent of the City’s population. Furthermore, 649 Piedmonters have received their second dose and are now fully vaccinated. Across Alameda County, almost 250,000 total vaccine doses have been administered and over 61,500 county residents have been fully vaccinated. On February 8, the county widened eligibility and began vaccinating people in Phase 1B Tier 1. This group includes people aged 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. This entire phase of people numbers approximately 325,000 residents countywide. The state defines the eligibility framework. Alameda County waited a few weeks before opening up eligibility to Phase 1B Tier 1 – the state allowed counties to begin vaccinating the latter phase on January 26. Alongside people in Phase 1B Tier 1, Phase 1A continues to be vaccinated. This phase, comprised of healthcare workers as well as the residents and staff of long-term care facilities, was the first group eligible when the first doses arrived in December. In Alameda County, Phase 1A includes an estimated 145,000 people. Eligible residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider or employer to receive a vaccination appointment. articles.text: Five new cases of COVID-19 reported in Piedmont One case of a more contagious strain of a COVID-19 variant was discovered in Alameda County, according to a report from the Alameda County Public Health Department on Wednesday, February 10. The variant, known to scientists as the B.1.351 variant of SARS-CoV-2, was first identified in South Africa last October. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has said that there is no evidence that this variant causes more severe symptoms, but data suggests it might spread more easily. The single case in Alameda County and another reported in Santa Clara County were the first cases of the South African variant reported in California. Details of the Alameda County case have not been released. “The case in Alameda County remains under investigation,” the County said. In the Santa Clara County case, however, the individual had recently returned from traveling internationally in mid-January. The individual and other members of the household followed the county’s 10-day mandatory travel quarantine and remained in their apartment. The cases were detected by genomic sequencing done through Stanford University. Since only a small fraction of COVID-19 cases are sequenced, it is possible that there are undetected cases of virus variants in the Bay Area. “The cases we share with you today are only the ones that have been confirmed through genomic sequencing,” Dr. Nicholas Moss, the Health Officer for Alameda County, said in a statement. “As we work quickly to learn more, our best defense right now is to stay vigilant and reduce transmission as much as possible. The more chances the virus has to spread, the more opportunities it has to adapt and create new variants. articles.text: He’s back! Neil Rothenberg, Piedmont High’s Hall of Fame tennis coach who was inducted in 2018, has come out of retirement for the 2021 season. “Don’t put much attention on me,” said Rothenberg with a laugh, diving quickly into the circumstances surrounding the upcoming 2021 season. “It’s about the team, but it’s going to be fun… I truly miss coaching; I just really enjoy high school and college tennis. For tennis at PHS, the unique challenge of operating during a pandemic has required both girls’ and boys’ tennis teams to play their seasons concurrently. That will require all hands on deck for a program that will continue to support JV teams for both boys and girls. “I’m glad to have his help,” said current coach Jim Landes, who was Rothenberg’s JV coach and stepped into the varsity role when Rothenberg retired on 2015. “We may have to do boys’ and girls’ simultaneously at different sites. It’s great to have Neil here.” Neil Rothenberg in an earlier photo. “He’s a great coach with a lot of experience. It’s really good news,” Landes added. The Highlanders are scheduled to face its four Foothill Division opponents: Alameda, Berkeley, Bishop O’Dowd, and Castro Valley. However, issues come with transportation to-and-from games, notably for away matches. There are questions that haven’t been answered yet, such as whether seniors can drive to the matches, because there is no carpooling allowed. That means that Tennis coaches Jim Landes [right] and Neil Rothenberg talk strategy at a recent practice. parents will have to drive their own kids. “There are a lot of things that have to be worked out,” he added. “We’re requesting the Park Courts in order to have a JV team.” Rothenberg, who strings racquets for the UC Berkeley tennis program, mentioned that Berkeley High may not even have a place to call home. “There are a lot of questions for other schools, too. Castro Valley and Berkeley have always had a difficult time with carpooling. And Berkeley High has an issue with courts. They are practicing at different times at Edwards Stadium (at UC Berkeley) and they are being very cautious. I don’t think the Berkeley Tennis Club will give up any courts for the matches. The members keep the courts pretty full most of the time,” said Rothenberg. Landes previously mentioned that the WACC (league) will allow teams to structure their own matches – meaning instead of splitting sites home and away, boys and girls could potentially have mixed doubles. “That is a possibility. As far as the league is concerned, anything is allowed as long as both coaches agree. I’m thinking we could even do a team-tennis format, where instead of five matches, it’s 10 matches. That would allow two mens’ and womens’ singles and doubles, two mixed doubles, or even more to the mix. Even speed tennis could be played,” mentioned Rothenberg. Rothenberg pointed out the hard work that Landes has put into keeping tennis alive in Piedmont. With all the questions surrounding classes, forming cohorts, and protocols for interscholastic sports, tennis has been the one constant for PHS athletes. Staff Photos Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame tennis coach Neil Rothenberg at his induction ceremony in 2018. Neil Rothenberg with assistant coach Corey Reich at his Hall of Fame induction. “That’s a big part of why we talked about coming back. This is a very unique season. The idea is to get these kids on the courts who have been pouring their heart and soul into the sport. What Jim has done to keep his programs going is just amazing,” said Rothenberg. Rothenberg retired after the 2015 season after taking the program after Ted Scherman and helping build it into a powerhouse tennis program known throughout Northern California. The Highlanders’ girls’ tennis team has won the league title for 19 consecutive years, a state record. When he retired in 2015, Rothenberg’s teams amassed a record of 501-103 and won three consecutive NCS Team titles. Although Rothenberg has been away from coaching, it may not seem that way for many of the players. The former coach always stayed close to the game; peering over matches and practice at the Corey Reich Tennis Center, often spotted on the corner of Bonita and Vista using the recycling can for VIP seating. Rothenberg, a natural baseball historian and fanatic, made sure to reference some specific comparisons to his return in Piedmont. “I feel like Tony La Russa and Jim Palmer,” said Rothenberg laughing, citing La Russa’s return to managing with the White Sox, while Palmer returned to pitching for the Orioles in 1991. “That’s where the comparisons stop, though.” In a time where nothing seems normal, some Piedmont High tennis greatness sounds like a refreshing course for the small town on the hill. articles.text: Photo courtesy of the Toronto Star Mackie McDonald reached the Round of 16 of the prestigious Grand Slam tournament, the Australian Open, defeating three Top-100 players in the process. The Pride of Piedmont, Mackenzie “Mackie” McDonald, reached the Round of 16 of the prestigious Australian Open for the second time in his career, upsetting three players before falling to the world’s No. 4 player, Daniil Medvedev in straight sets on Sunday, February 14. His journey in the Grand Slam tournament made his hometown – and fans everywhere – proud. It matched his longest appearance in a Grand Slam tournament, the Wimbledon’s Round of 16 in 2018. He was the only American player left in Australia Open last week. Mackie upset No. 22 Borna Coric of Croatia on Wednesday, February 10 in four sets, 6-4, 6-2, 4-6, 6-4, and followed up with a straight-set victory over South Africa’s Lloyd Harris, 7-6 (9-7), 6-1, 6-4, who entered as the world’s No. 91 ranked player. Reaching the rarified air of the Round of 16 was justification for the 25-year old professional. Making his fourth Australian Open appearance and the first Grand Slam of 2021 carried vindication after his long recovery from a severe hamstring injury that caused him to miss nearly all of 2019. “I’m proud of making the Round of 16 at the Australian Open to kick off the year! This result means a lot to me knowing how hard I’ve worked to get back to the highest level of tennis after an injury. I’m looking forward to continuing to improve and setting the bar higher,” said McDonald on his official social media. His injury was bad enough to end many careers, a torn hamstring tendon off the bone. And for Mackie, a speedster whose maneuverability on the court characterized his game, 2020 proved to be a process in finding his form. The injury catapulted him from a young pro on the rise into a veteran on the tour. After climbing to No. 57 in the ATP rankings in April 2019, McDonald suffered an injury a month later at the French Open. He then dipped to No. 132 when recovering from injury for last year’s Australian Open. Now more than a year later, McDonald’s current ranking of No. 192 will undoubtedly be changed after handing three Top-100 ATP veterans one-sided defeats. He opened the Aussie Open with a four-set win over No. 82 Marco Cecchinato (3-6, 6-3, 6-2, 6-2) on Monday, February 8. The cards were highest stacked against him in his Feb. 10 second-round match against No. 22 Coric – who had his own Croatian fan-section in a tournament that was supposedly only open to Australian Open officials. McDonald was lights-out against Coric, sending 13 aces with a percentage of 11.3 and won 71 percent of his first serves. Keeping Coric running left to right on the baseline, McDonald caused 53 unforced errors from his Croatian counterpart. The man from Piedmont went into Round Three against Harris as a slight underdog, but once again he absolutely dominated his opponent in straight sets. McDonald had 12 aces and won 81 percent of his first serves to go along with five break points. He also forced Harris into 44 errors. His running forehand was on display against Harris, striking several winners that kept the 6-foot, 5-inch South African struggling to find a comeback. It marked a career-high run in three Grand Slam matches for McDonald. The Australian Open has proven to be a tournament where Mackie appears to be at his best. He burst onto the scene in the 2018 Australian Open as an unknown kid out of UCLA, nearly upsetting No. 3 Grigor Dimitrov in five sets of the Aussie Open’s Round of 64. In 2019, McDonald upset No. 8 ranked Andrey Rublev in four sets, but lost in four to No. 43 Marin Cilic. He played No. 33 ranked Daniel Evans in the 2020 Australian Open, losing in five sets after taking the first two sets, 3-6, 4-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-3.

By Jonathan Comeaux The Pride of Piedmont, Mackenzie “Mackie” McDonald, reached the Round of 16 of the prestigious Australian Open for the second time in his career, upsetting three players before falling to the world’s No. 4 player, Daniil Medvedev in straight sets on Sunday, February 14. His journey in the Grand Slam tournament made his hometown – and fans everywhere – proud. It matched his longest appearance in a Grand Slam tournament, the Wimbledon’s Round of 16 in 2018. He was the only American player left in Australia Open last week. Mackie upset No. 22 Borna Coric of Croatia on Wednesday, February 10 in four sets, 6-4, 6-2, 4-6, 6-4, and followed up with a straight-set victory over South Africa’s Lloyd Harris, 7-6 (9-7), 6-1, 6-4, who entered as the world’s No. 91 ranked player. Reaching the rarified air of the Round of 16 was justification for the 25-year old professional. Making his fourth Australian Open appearance and the first Grand Slam of 2021 carried vindication after his long recovery from a severe hamstring injury that caused him to miss nearly all of 2019. “I’m proud of making the Round of 16 at the Australian Open to kick off the year! This result means a lot to me knowing how hard I’ve worked to get back to the highest level of tennis after an injury. I’m looking forward to continuing to improve and setting the bar higher,” said McDonald on his official social media. His injury was bad enough to end many careers, a torn hamstring tendon off the bone. And for Mackie, a speedster whose maneuverability on the court characterized his game, 2020 proved to be a process in finding his form. The injury catapulted him from a young pro on the rise into a veteran on the tour. After climbing to No. 57 in the ATP rankings in April 2019, McDonald suffered an injury a month later at the French Open. He then dipped to No. 132 when recovering from injury for last year’s Australian Open. Now more than a year later, McDonald’s current ranking of No. 192 will undoubtedly be changed after handing three Top-100 ATP veterans one-sided defeats. He opened the Aussie Open with a four-set win over No. 82 Marco Cecchinato (3-6, 6-3, 6-2, 6-2) on Monday, February 8. The cards were highest stacked against him in his Feb. 10 second-round match against No. 22 Coric – who had his own Croatian fan-section in a tournament that was supposedly only open to Australian Open officials. McDonald was lights-out against Coric, sending 13 aces with a percentage of 11.3 and won 71 percent of his first serves. Keeping Coric running left to right on the baseline, McDonald caused 53 unforced errors from his Croatian counterpart. The man from Piedmont went into Round Three against Harris as a slight underdog, but once again he absolutely dominated his opponent in straight sets. McDonald had 12 aces and won 81 percent of his first serves to go along with five break points. He also forced Harris into 44 errors. His running forehand was on display against Harris, striking several winners that kept the 6-foot, 5-inch South African struggling to find a comeback. It marked a career-high run in three Grand Slam matches for McDonald. The Australian Open has proven to be a tournament where Mackie appears to be at his best. He burst onto the scene in the 2018 Australian Open as an unknown kid out of UCLA, nearly upsetting No. 3 Grigor Dimitrov in five sets of the Aussie Open’s Round of 64. In 2019, McDonald upset No. 8 ranked Andrey Rublev in four sets, but lost in four to No. 43 Marin Cilic. He played No. 33 ranked Daniel Evans in the 2020 Australian Open, losing in five sets after taking the first two sets, 3-6, 4-6, 6-1, 6-2, 6-3. More than 10,000 people participate in this free self-guided hiking and bicycling program to explore the East Bay regional parks and to keep fit outdoors. Each year the Trails Challenge highlights 20 trails for all abilities. Trails include easy, moderate, and challenging routes; many with scenic destinations in a variety of parklands and shorelines, according to the District’s website. Earn a commemorative pin by accomplishing five of its listed trails or 26.2 miles of walking within their parks. 2021 Trail Challenge Guidebook (https://www.ebparks.org/civicax/filebank/blobdload.aspx?blobid=33795). East Bay Regional’s 20 listed parks range from Easy, Moderate, and Challenging. Their Staff Photo A view of the French Trail in Redwood Regional Park. guidebook provides useful information on each destination like total mileage, elevation gain, and whether dogs are permitted, while also mentioning features and highlights of each trail. The Park District is featuring two trails near Piedmont, Redwood Regional’s Stream to French trails—listed as moderate, and a 7.9-mile loop through Tilden Park, rated as challenging. The full list of the 20 trails can be found at: https://www.ebparks. org/TC This intrepid writer decided to tackle the closest trail to home. Rated moderate, the Redwood Regional path is a 6.2-mile loop with an elevation gain of 967 feet. The hike starts at the Canyon Meadow Staging Area off of Redwood Road, going two miles along the Stream Trail until intersecting with the Tres Sendas Trail, which jolts up 332 feet in elevation to the French Trail. Along the Stream Trail is ladybug season, about 1.5 miles in are bushels of ladybugs that gather during the winter months. Scientists note that this behavior is a way for the species to reproduce and to cope with a limited winter food supply. On every branch, post, and rock are swarms of ladybugs piling on one another, laying eggs on the underside of leaves. “Here in Redwood, they wait out the winter, often along the creeks,” wrote East Bay Regional Parks on their informative panel. “They are likely attracted to the area by chemicals in the air, or from pheromones, or scent markers, left behind in their footprints.” The walk along the French Trail goes 2.5 miles until intersecting with the Orchard Trail to take hikers back to their car at Canyon Meadows.

articles.text: Murietta Falls in Del Valle Regional Park in Livermore A bit of the steep uphill section toward Murietta Falls. How about discovering a waterfall barely one hour from Piedmont? Murietta Falls, located in Del Valle Regional Park in Livermore, awaits you. It is considered the highest waterfall in the Bay Area at an elevation of 3,000 feet in the Ohlone Wilderness. A small stream cascades over a 199- foot cliff to create the waterfall. This destination requires lots of legwork; a trip of slightly over six miles outand-back, or six miles overall with about 4,100 feet in elevation gain. The prize of Murietta Falls is well worth the grind. Hikers would be wise to come early given this trail will require 6-7 hours of hiking. Showing up at 11:30 a.m. meant that this reporter was nearly the last hiker to leave the park. We passed 53 people, all but two on the trek toward the waterfall. The Ohlone Wilderness Trail stretches for 28 miles and is known as a popular backpacking area for overnight hikers. The trail to Murietta Falls starts across the bridge on Del Valle Road, heading down the blocked off road to the Sailor Camp Trail, which eventually becomes the Ohlone Wilderness Trail. Follow the red Ohlone Wilderness Trail markers on each trail post. The hike begins with a bang, with 1,150 feet in the first half mile, then a level area in the next half-mile so you can catch your breath. But then another jolt of nearly 1,200 feet in elevation gain takes place in the next 1.3 miles. That means over 2,300 feet in elevation gain over the first 2.3 miles of the trail with some gradients above 20 percent. Picking up 1,000 feet per mile is an arduous task that will prepare hikers for the toughest of challenges. For instance, the SF Chronicle’s most difficult trail in the Bay Area, Mt. Diablo’s Burma Road Trail, has an equally difficult two-mile elevation trial. But you’re not done. The 3-mile mark means trail goers will embark on the final climb to the falls after descending over a small creek. After passing the creek, you begin another ascent of 1,530 feet over the next 1.5 miles. After the final climb, the trail opens up to a valley, turning right past Johnny’s Pond. This means you have less than a mile to Murietta Falls, finally! The creek wraps through a rocky gulch and over the near 100-foot cliff face. The hike back to the car has much less ascent and is quicker. Hikers will face a climb of around 350 feet walking back, with one more uphill challenge of around 500 feet—but aside from those two sections, it is mostly downhill. Follow the red trail markers to stay on the Ohlone Wilderness Trail. Once past the creek, moss covers nearly everything in sight. Johnny’s Pond on the right means you’re on the homestretch to Murietta Falls.

articles.text: A scene from San Francisco Ballet’s Midsummer Night’s Dream. Dance review by Paul Hertelendy Shakespeare and ballet usually means Romeo and Juliet. But there’s more. For a rare in-depth look at George Balanchine going back to his Russian roots, check out his lavish Midsummer Night’s Dream on a stream at San Francisco Ballet. It’s a stunning phalanx of 50 or more perfectly attuned dancers, a spectacle of palatial elegance and dance perfection. If only it had similar sparkle or propulsion. We regard Balanchine as a great, one of the fathers of modern ballet. In this 1962 “Dream” however he reverted to the spirit of 19th-century Petipa days back in St. Petersburg, executed beautifully, as if you were coming upon a room full of rare china and crystal chandeliers. At first glance it’s a show to take the kids to, as much as Nutcracker. But the humor and whimsey are in short supply, even with that cutup Puck cavorting about the stage doing his boyish magical mischief. The convoluted madness of the Shakespearean plot is crammed in the first half, where a large cast plays out the fantasy of mismatched lovers, the result of a magical flower radically reorienting every one’s love interest in zany ways. Only a true Shakespearean can tell apart the soloistic ladies – Hermia, Helena, Hyppolyta, Titania – or tell which truly belongs paired off with Lysander, Theseus, Oberon or Demetrius. The philandering Puck can scramble the lineup of lovers with glee until finally the bumpkin Bottom is turned into a donkey, sought after as the ludicrous ardent love object of the spellbound, queenly Titania. Both Balanchine and Sir Frederick Ashton did ballet versions of Shakespeare’s Dream in the 1960s to grace each side of the Atlantic. Both use as foundation stone Mendelssohn’s score embodying some of the most deft tone-painting of any German-romantic music. The biggest difference lay in the role of the donkey – in Ashton, farcically pawing a hoof on the ground to accompany the asinine “bray” in the priceless score, while in Balanchine playing a dignified, gentleman-like role with halting steps – at least, as dignified as that giant donkey’s head would permit. In addition, Ashton created a one-act performance, while Balanchine made it evening-length, adding snippets of other Mendelssohn as needed, particularly for the grand but soulless ballet spectacle in breathtaking glittering costumes that makes up the old-line act-two divertissements. Curiously enough, for the balletomane the high point comes in the lengthy and highly demanding act two pas de deux, done here by Frances Chung with Ulrik Birkkjaer. Each time you think they will wilt in this nonstop seven-minute duo, they come back with yet more arabesques and lifts with an Olympian energy. It is a breathtaking tour de force that, in streaming, you might want to view over and over. The take-away here is the near-infinite depth of SF Ballet, even in a casting devoid of some of the top company stars. It’s as if the troupe defies you to find any weakness in the endless lead parts, whether Sasha De Sola (Titania), Elizabeth Powell (Hermia) or Sarah Van Patten (Helena), or alternatively Luke Ingham (Demetrius), Esteban Hernandez (Oberon), Myles Thatcher (Lysander), Tiit Helimets (Theseus) or that endearing man-donkey Bottom, played by Lucas Erni. The spell-caster Puck was Cavan Conley, more mischief than merriment. The national backgrounds of these were most diverse: Mexico, Argentina, Estonia, Canada, Denmark, Australia, USA. Of note in a tour-de-force role leading the hunters was the athletic Sasha Mukhamedov playing Hyppolyta – part Amazon, part archer. Uniquely, at the end, she could take her bow while carting her bow. Martin West led the pit orchestra, to which my meager laptop speakers cannot do justice. San Francisco Ballet in Balanchine’s 1962 Midsummer Night’s Dream, filmed at the S.F. Opera House in March 2020. Now available on streaming. This and other streams are available by subscription online. To view, visit www.sfballet.org, or call (415) 865-2000.

articles.text: The California Shakespeare Theatre, commonly known as Cal Shakes, has announced that its 2021 Season will be called a Season of Shared Light, and will include community groups, artists, and arts and culture organizations from across the Bay Area. The decision was made in response to the ongoing pandemic and movement for racial equity in the arts and beyond. “At Cal Shakes, many of our performances take place—not in the relative anonymity of a dark theater—but under the sun,” noted Artistic Director Eric Ting. “It’s a thing I’ve come to love, and now miss dearly – the actors and audience alike in full view of one another, relinquishing the control we normally associate with the theater and instead navigating the complexity of each other’s very real presence across the arc of a performance, cohabiting the shared light of our space.” Cal Shakes will produce only one play in its 47th season, The Winter’s Tale by William Shakespeare, to be directed by Ting. In addition, the theatre company will continue to develop digital and in-person programming, safety permitting, throughout 2021, including Shakespeare In-Depth with Philippa Kelly, its Direct Address series, and other performance and educational opportunities. “Over the next few months we’ll be sharing the fruits of that labor - a developing vision of mutual aid rooted in creative expression and collective action,” Ting added. This summer, Cal Shakes plans to share its open-air venue with Bay Area arts organizations, to include West Edge Opera, Destiny Arts, and Bandaloop. “We know that outdoor space will continue to be a premium in 2021, so sharing our grounds with our fellow arts and cultural organizations feels like exactly the thing we should be doing this year,“ Managing Director Sarah Williams said. “We are eagerly looking forward to the summer, and operating under the assumption that by May we will be able to responsibly return in some capacity. Above all, we will continue to be flexible and monitor the mandates around reopening to ensure the safety of our artists, staff, and community.” Due to the ongoing pandemic and uncertainties surrounding it, Cal Shakes is holding off on announcing specific dates and ticket sales for The Winter’s Tale until there is more clarity around re-opening, gathering, and social distancing guidelines. All events are subject to change. Further artistic and community initiatives as part of the Season of Shared Light will be announced over the coming months. For information visit www. calshakes.org.

articles.text: The first episode of the new season of “Aurora Connects” is “The Vietnamese-American Experience,” featuring guests Oanh Nguyen, Linda Nguyen, and Trieu Tran. Williams has been Aurora’s Associate Artistic Director since August 2019. pages.text: 16 Wednesday, February 17, 2021 Arts & Entertainment The Ballet turns to Shakespeare A scene from San Francisco Ballet’s Midsummer Night’s Dream. Dance review by Paul Hertelendy Shakespeare and ballet usually means Romeo and Juliet. But there’s more. For a rare in-depth look at George Balanchine going back to his Russian roots, check out his lavish Midsummer Night’s Dream on a stream at San Francisco Ballet. It’s a stunning phalanx of 50 or more perfectly attuned dancers, a spectacle of palatial elegance and dance perfection. If only it had similar sparkle or propulsion. We regard Balanchine as a great, one of the fathers of modern ballet. In this 1962 “Dream” however he reverted to the spirit of 19th-century Petipa days back in St. Petersburg, executed beautifully, as if you were coming upon a room full of rare china and crystal chandeliers. At first glance it’s a show to take the kids to, as much as Nutcracker. But the humor and whimsey are in short supply, even with that cutup Puck cavorting about the stage doing his boyish magical mischief. The convoluted madness of the Shakespearean plot is crammed in the first half, where a large cast plays out the fantasy of mismatched lovers, the result of a magical flower radically reorienting every one’s love interest in zany ways. Only a true Shakespearean can tell apart the soloistic ladies – Hermia, Helena, Hyppolyta, Titania – or tell which truly belongs paired off with Lysander, Theseus, Oberon or Demetrius. The philandering Puck can scramble the lineup of lovers with glee until finally the bumpkin Bottom is turned into a donkey, sought after as the ludicrous ardent love object of the spellbound, queenly Titania. Both Balanchine and Sir Frederick Ashton did ballet versions of Shakespeare’s Dream in the 1960s to grace each side of the Atlantic. Both use as foundation stone Mendelssohn’s score embodying some of the most deft tone-painting of any German-romantic music. The biggest difference lay in the role of the donkey – in Ashton, farcically pawing a hoof on the ground to accompany the asinine “bray” in the priceless score, while in Balanchine playing a dignified, gentleman-like role with halting steps – at least, as dignified as that giant donkey’s head would permit. In addition, Ashton created a one-act performance, while Balanchine made it evening-length, adding snippets of other Mendelssohn as needed, particularly for the grand but soulless ballet spectacle in breathtaking glittering costumes that makes up the old-line act-two divertissements. Curiously enough, for the balletomane the high point comes in the lengthy and highly demanding act two pas de deux, done here by Frances Chung with Ulrik Birkkjaer. Each time you think they will wilt in this nonstop seven-minute duo, they come back with yet more arabesques and lifts with an Olympian energy. It is a breathtaking tour de force that, in streaming, you might want to view over and over. The take-away here is the near-infinite depth of SF Ballet, even in a casting devoid of some of the top company stars. It’s as if the troupe defies you to find any weakness in the endless lead parts, whether Sasha De Sola (Titania), Elizabeth Powell (Hermia) or Sarah Van Patten (Helena), or alternatively Luke Ingham (Demetrius), Esteban Hernandez (Oberon), Myles Thatcher (Lysander), Tiit Helimets (Theseus) or that endearing man-donkey Bottom, played by Lucas Erni. The spell-caster Puck was Cavan Conley, more mischief than merriment. The national backgrounds of these were most diverse: Mexico, Argentina, Estonia, Canada, Denmark, Australia, USA. Of note in a tour-de-force role leading the hunters was the athletic Sasha Mukhamedov playing Hyppolyta – part Amazon, part archer. Uniquely, at the end, she could take her bow while carting her bow. Martin West led the pit orchestra, to which my meager laptop speakers cannot do justice. San Francisco Ballet in Balanchine’s 1962 Midsummer Night’s Dream, filmed at the S.F. California Shakespeare Theatre to produce The Winter’s Tale this summer By Allyson Aleksey The California Shakespeare Theatre, commonly known as Cal Shakes, has announced that its 2021 Season will be called a Season of Shared Light, and will include community groups, artists, and arts and culture organizations from across the Bay Area. The decision was made in response to the ongoing pandemic and movement for racial equity in the arts and beyond. “At Cal Shakes, many of our performances take place—not in the relative anonymity of a dark theater—but under the sun,” noted Artistic Director Eric Ting. “It’s a thing I’ve come to love, and now miss dearly – the actors and audience alike in full view of one another, relinquishing the control we normally associate with the theater and instead navigating the complexity of each other’s very real presence across the arc of a performance, cohabiting the shared light of our space.” Cal Shakes will produce only one play in its 47th season, The Winter’s Tale by William Shakespeare, to be directed by Ting. In addition, the theatre company will continue to develop digital and in-person programming, safety permitting, throughout 2021, including Shakespeare In-Depth with Philippa Kelly, its Direct Address series, and other performance and educational opportunities. “Over the next few months we’ll be sharing the fruits of that labor - a developing vision of mutual aid rooted in creative expression and collective action,” Ting added. This summer, Cal Shakes plans to share its open-air venue with Bay Area arts organizations, to include West Edge Opera, Destiny Arts, and Bandaloop. “We know that outdoor space will continue to be a premium in 2021, so sharing our grounds with our fellow arts and cultural organizations feels like exactly the thing we should be doing this year,“ Managing Director Sarah Williams said. “We are eagerly looking forward to the summer, and operating under the assumption that by May we will be able to responsibly return in some capacity. Above all, we will continue to be flexible and monitor the mandates around reopening to ensure the safety of our artists, staff, and community.” Due to the ongoing pandemic and uncertainties surrounding it, Cal Shakes is holding off on announcing specific dates and ticket sales for The Winter’s Tale until there is more clarity around re-opening, gathering, and social distancing guidelines. All events are subject to change. Further artistic and community initiatives as part of the Season of Shared Light will be announced over the coming months. For information visit www. calshakes.org. articles.text: The San Francisco Maritime National Historic Park and the Maritime Museum will host a virtual concert of maritime songs and sea chanties from Black traditions of the United States and West Indies. The online event will be held on Saturday, February 27, and will feature four performers: Ron and Natalie Daise, Richard Adrianowicz, and Peter Kasin. The Daises, originally from South Carolina, are writers, actors, educators, and internationally renowned television performers. From 1994 to 1998, the husband-and-wife team starred in Nick Jr. TV’s award-winning “Gullah Gullah Island,” for which they also served as cultural consultants. The show was cited by TV Guide as one of the “10 best children’s shows” in 1996. They were nominees for two NAACP Image Awards and a Daytime Emmy Award. Adrianowicz’s interest in traditional music began in the early 70s when he moved from Chicago to California. He was part of several groups in the San Francisco Bay Area, including “Out of the Rain.” Adrianowicz is one of the regular shanty singers at Hyde Street Pier’s monthly shanty sings in San Francisco, held Natalie and Ron Daise aboard one of the historic sailing ships moored there. In 2002, he released Time Ashore is Over, a recording of sea shanties and sea songs featuring a chorus of singers from Hyde Street Pier. Peter Kasin, raised in Berkeley, took a strong interest in sea music after having first attended one of the monthly chanty sings in late 1989. He organizes sea music concerts and festivals in San Francisco. The event will begin at 11 a.m. and will run about 90 minutes. The virtual concert is free, but donations are welcome. Visit https://maritime.org/eventshome/afroseamusicconcert/ to reserve your spot.

articles.text: Piedmont blues guitarist Jules Leyhe brings his band to Piedmont Piano in February 25 for a 5 p.m. concert. Jules Leyhe and the Family Jules Band makes its first appearance at Piedmont Piano on Thursday, February 25 at 5 p.m. The concert is virtual, and can be viewed on YouTube or Facebook. Leyhe’s band is a high-energy blues quartet of some of Oakland’s greatest blues and jazz musicians. The ensemble’s blend of funky, blues and soul inspired improvisation makes for a highly entertaining performance you won’t want to miss. Leyhe, a native of Piedmont, is a blues guitarist specializing in slide guitar. The band includes Nancy Wright on saxophone, Ian McArdle on keyboards and bass, and Isaac Schwartz on drums. Improvisation is at the core of this band’s soul, always taking advantage of each bandmate’s playful ears and pushing each other’s abilities to the edge seeking a new sound over traditional styles of music like blues and soul. articles.text: Katherine Heigl and Josh Duhamel star in Life As We Know It. Movie review by Chris Honoré Life as We Know It is so solidly formulaic that it should be taught to budding screenwriters as the quintessential contemporary romantic comedy (rom-com). It is a slick and predictable film, absent any real depth. Here’s how a rom-com is set up: couple meets cute or not so cute. In this film, it’s not so cute. Holly Berenson (Katherine Heigl) and Eric Messer (Josh Duhamel), are set up on a blind date by their best friends, Peter and Alison (Hayes MacArthur and Christina Hendricks). Instantly they discover they are oil and water. He is a jock with arrested development, irresponsible, a womanizer, and – what else? – rides a motorcycle. Holly is responsible, runs a bakery shop, and has had precious few dates for reasons that are never clearly explained. Because Peter and Alison include them in family events, especially the first birthday party for their daughter, Sophie, Messer (as he’s called) and Holly have multiple opportunities to reinforce their disdain for one another. And then the dark hammer falls (this is all in the trailer). Peter and Alison are killed in a car accident. Messer and Holly are told by the family attorney that according to the will they are Sophie’s designated co-guardians and, if they agree, must live in the family home and raise her together. Let the games begin. According to the formula, their mutual distaste for one another runs headlong into their commitment to Sophie. Naturally, since this is a rom-com, there are lots of issues, some slightly comedic. There’s even a crisis that results in a separation. But this film long ago telegraphed the ending. It’s just a matter of waiting and watching as two attractive people solve and resolve their differences while discovering that all that anger just might be reframed into something far more positive. As formula rom-coms go, Life as We Know It is good enough and follows nicely in the tradition of Baby Boom and Three Men and a Baby. It’s easy to watch with good-looking people who were looking for love in all the wrong places. Until now. Life as We Know It. Directed by Greg Berlanti. Starring Katherine Heigl, Josh Lucas, and Josh Duhamel. Rated PG-13.
articles.title: Life as We Know It a pleasant romantic comedy

articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Churchill is an intimate character study of a man who stood, however imperfectly, at the crossroads of history. A man (wonderfully portrayed by Brian Cox) who had defiantly held the people of England together through its darkest hours – a time of the London Blitz in the early part of World War II. The toll it took on that island nation’s people remains indescribable. Germany was relentless and indiscriminate, delivered nightly bombing raids that killed thousands. However, as D-Day began to take shape (referred to as Operation Overlord), according to this docudrama, Churchill’s emotions began to fray. He gradually concluded that his generals’ plans would result in untold carnage and result in the Allies losing the war. And so, he began to do battle with the generals. He confronted Gen. Dwight Eisenhower of the U.S. (John Slatterly), and England’s Gen. Bernard Montgomery (Julian Wadham) with his doubts, often haranguing them, questioning their tactics. He argued for diversionary battles to the north and south of Normandy. He was drinking too much, and treated those close to him shabbily, to include his wife Clementine (played by the always wonderful Miranda Richardson). While Eisenhower and Montgomery were unyielding in their commitment to carry through with plans for the invasion of Normandy Beach in June 1944, they waited, the weather being their only consideration. Churchill agonized and even prayed for a massive storm. Suddenly, after being central to England’s survival he was now required to sit on the sideline, powerless to influence events. It was not a role he could abide. He was also haunted by his very personal memories of the battle of Gallipoli in world War I where more than 200,000 English troops perished, a campaign he had supported and led and one which he regretted all of his life. He was convinced that D-Day would be a repetition and it felt unendurable. What he did not realize was that while he was still fighting WWI, the generals were embarking on a historic invasion unlike anything the world had ever seen. Finally, of course, Churchill yields and gives a memorable, historic speech to the people of England on the day of the invasion. Whether Anglophiles may take exception to the portrayal of Churchill in this film, it is still engaging. It demonstrates that while Churchill remains a legend, he was to the good fortune of England the right man at the right moment in history. He was fundamentally a tower of strength and intelligence, though flawed. Churchill. Directed by Jonathan Teplitzky. Starring Brian Cox, Miranda Richardson and John Slatterly. 1 hr., 50 min. Rated PG. John Slatterly as Dwight Eisenhower, Danny Web as Alan Brooke, and Brian Cox as Winston Churchill in Churchill.
articles.title: Churchill – the story leading up to D-Day in WWII

Movie review by Chris Honoré Let’s assume that if the live-action reboot of Dumbo was going to soar at the box office, as did the original 1941 animated feature, then the Disney producers and writers paused and said something akin to, “The kids loved Dumbo in 1941; but that was then, and this is now.” A small toddler of an elephant with big blue eyes and enormous ears, soaring through the big top and buzzing the audience might not work. The kids in the audience are weaned on Marvel and DC superheroes, veterans of films replete with state-of-the-art CGI that is only limited by the writers’ imaginations. These kids have been there, done that. So how can the screenwriters take a small, adorable, semi-orphaned pachyderm and create a sequel that will engage kids, each hoping to be not only wowed, but touched by the story to the point of caring about Dumbo. So, the writers open with two children, Milly and Joe (Nico Parker, Finley Hobbins) who have just lost their mother to the flu pandemic of 1919. Happily, their father, Holt (Colin Farrell), though missing an arm from an injury in World War I, .has recently returned to the circus, and to them. And then begins Dumbo in earnest. The year is 1919. The place is Sarasota, Florida, and the circus is in town. It’s owned by a hyperbolic Max Medici (Danny DeVito). It’s a small, shoestring operation, a collection of society’s flotsam and jetsam all working for a slightly frayed Big Top. The wagons are paint-peeling tired, the elephants mistreated. Even Jumbo’s mom, pregnant, is about to be returned to a previous owner, since Max is unhappy with the price he paid. That is until Dumbo is born and spreads his ears while holding a feather, cheered on by Milly and Joe while Max sees his circus’ salvation. Director Tim Burton, for all of the steampunk color and 19th century texture, soon folds the small Medici Circus featuring Dumbo, into a much larger Coney Island/Disneyesque operation. It’s now called Dreamland, much of it decidedly not kid-friendly, headed by the villainous V.A. Vandervere (Michael Keaton), who is accompanied by his aerialist companion, Collette (Eva Green). The plan is to exploit Dumbo no matter the cost or outcome. When Vandervere discovers that Dumbo’s mother is locked up on the amusement park’s grounds and is an unnecessary distraction for little Dumbo, his solution is to put Jumbo down. Meanwhile, Milly and Joe and their dad, Holt, all seem helpless, as if pushed to the background, until finally they and the Medici crew set about executing a plan to rescue both Jumbo and Dumbo. This proves to be a precarious operation, one that stirs some real excitement. Regrettably, the final scenes of Dumbo seem almost an afterthought, with a quick nod to the environment when Jumbo and Dumbo are put onto a steamship and returned to their natural habitat somewhere in India. A nice thought needing a bit more explanation. Dumbo. Starring Colin Farrell, Eva Green, Michael Keaton and Danny DeVito. Directed by Tim Burton. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG. articles.text: Movie review by Chris Honoré Secretariat is a Disney film about a magnificent chestnut racehorse nicknamed Big Red, but more formally known as Secretariat, considered by many as the greatest racehorse of all time. In 1973 Red won the Triple Crown of racing – the Kentucky Derby, the Preakness and the Belmont Stakes. It was then, and remains still, the Holy Grail of horse racing, a trifecta that is rarely attained. No one does movies about animals better than Disney and Secretariat is filled with excitement: tight shots of jockeys clutching the reins as horses weighing some 1,200 pounds charge around an oval track more than a mile long. It’s intense, even thrilling. Of course, it’s irresistible for Disney not to give Secretariat a sentient intelligence. In one scene, Penny Chenery (Diane Lane), owner of Secretariat, stands holding the horse’s bridle, looking the horse in the eyes, while he looks and conveys to Penny that he’s ready to race. Disney loves to anthropomorphize animals (Bambi, et al); however, thankfully, director Randall Wallace shows restraint. A horse by any other name is still a horse. While the hub of the film is Secretariat and his ability to run, the focus throughout is on Penny, a Denver suburban housewife who tenaciously, with grit, takes a huge gamble on Secretariat when others in the old boys’ network suggest that she is a fool. It’s only because of her determination that she not only manages to keep control of her father’s Meadow Farms, in Doswell, Va., but enters Secretariat in races that will eventually lead to the Triple Crown. Disney has always been enamored with Jiminy Cricket characters like Penny (animated or otherwise) who wish upon a star, insisting it makes no difference who you are, while believing that dreams can come true. That theme is woven through countless Disney films, animated and not. It’s a nice thought and has resonated with audiences for more half a century. The real treat in this film is watching Diane Lane make the character of Penny Chenery her own. Lane is a hugely gifted actress, nominated for an Oscar for her performance in Unfaithful (a tour de force film for her). In this case, she carries Secretariat from the first frame. Lane is helped by the enormously talented actor John Malkovich portraying Lucien Laurin, the colorful French-Canadian trainer, and Margo Martindale as the longtime family secretary. Both are exceptional character actors. Malkovich’s breakthrough film was Places in the Heart. Secretariat is top-drawer family entertainment, especially for kids, say, eight and older. Adults will also be engaged by the sometimes sentimental yet compelling story of this remarkable horse and its equally remarkable owner. Secretariat. Directed by Randall Wallace, Starring Diane Lane, John Malkovich, Scott Glenn, and Margo Martindale. Rated PG. Diane Lane, John Malkovich and Margo Martindale in Disney’s Secretariat.
articles.title: Disney’s Secretariat a treat from start to finish

articles.text: Piedmont Center for the Arts has announced the addition of Aparna Rao to its Board of Directors, made effective on February 16. Most recently Rao served as the Interim Executive Director for Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir and is a choir parent. She holds a diverse range of experience in law, marketing, media, design and corporate charitable giving. She worked as a production intern for Michael Krasny at KQED, and as a Marketing Assistant at Pioneer Investments and Fleet Bank, both in Boston. She has served as a lecturer at UC Berkeley since 2000. She has a Bachelor of Arts in Philosophy from Brandeis University and a Masters of Arts equivalent in Philosophy from Cal. “I wholeheartedly believe in the importance of the arts and respect PCA’s mission to offer artists an affordable space to share their work with Piedmont and, more broadly, Bay Area residents. There is something truly beautiful in having a center for community to coalesce around the arts,” Rao said. “I am particularly moved by the board’s current commitment of reaching out to a larger group of artists that reflect the diversity of the greater Bay Area. I hope that the connections I have made to arts organization directors, diverse artists, arts educators and arts journalists through my experience as Interim Executive Director of the Piedmont ChilAparna Rao dren’s Choir, and as an Oakland artisan will prove to be an asset.” PCA President Sue Malick said that Rao will extend the center’s reach for contacts in the greater Bay Area arts community. “We are so delighted to have Aparna as a member of the board. I got to know her when she served as the Interim Executive Director for Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. Her enthusiasm, leadership, devotion to the arts and her connections throughout the Bay Area will be a strong addition to the board,” Malick said. “When I interviewed Aparna Rao and reviewed her background, I was impressed by her commitment to a wide range of artistic endeavors. Her leadership of Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir, her work as an artisan, and her training in the management of non-profit arts organizations made her an ideal person to add to the Board of Directors of the Piedmont Center for the Arts,” said PCA board member Tom Reicher.

articles.text: Jazz pianist Chick Corea Jazz great Chick Corea died last week. You don’t need to be a jazz aficionado to appreciate his art. You see, he represented and lived the best of humanity. Lofty dedication like this is often the sphere of a religious person. I do not know if Corea was a religious person, but with his devotion he easily could have been a Sunday school teacher. One of my friends is a very insightful music critic. He is also a fine jazz pianist. Naturally, I asked my friend Richard Ginell if he had any contact with Chick Corea. Yes he did, and his observations were insightful to say the least. The first thing that impressed me was that Chick Corea was also an excellent classical pianist. He recorded Mozart piano concertos and was very adept at Gershwin’s Rhapsody in Blue. Just that by itself is impressive enough. All I need to do is quote him a little bit and his words speak directly to the heart and to the intellect. His music does not need an intermediary – music never does. articles.text: Haiku contest finalists drew inspiration from Filoli’s winter blooms. Filoli House and Garden, located in Woodside, conducted a haiku contest that asked for submissions inspired by Filoli’s winter blooms. Winners were announced via Zoom and social media platforms on Valentine’s Day. A special guest judge, San Mateo County Poet Laureate Aileen Cassinetto, read the winning poem. Here is a sample of the finalists: Down the garden path wild turkey’s feathers shimmer in the winter sun –Alliana Lili Yang The soft hum of wings darting among the flowers seeking winter blooms –Lydia Becker In the white petals, crinkled cups holding yellow centers, a bee dines –LiAnn Yim The sky wept softly over hedges rust, poppies white such grace in fallow times –Heather Bourbeau To read all haiku finalists and winners, visit https://filoli.org/ haiku/.

articles.text: Sometimes people ask me, a bit incredulously, how can a librarian work from home? These days I help with sidewalk service at the Asian Branch Library three days a week, and the other days I work from home. I can tell you how a librarian works from home. Besides purchasing children’s books for you to pick up at sidewalk service and online tasks like training and responding to e-mail, I meet children where they are – on Zoom. In pre-COVID days, teachers at Piedmont Avenue Elementary School would bring their classes to the Piedmont Ave. library for a fun hour of chaos: I would read them a story, kids would scramble about finding books to borrow, and then they would rush back to school. Class visits on Zoom are similarly hilarious but without the tangible satisfaction of putting books into students’ hands. In a typical visit with a class, I’ll log into the teacher’s Zoom room, read the kids a book, show them my online virtual reading room, talk about sidewalk service or another library resource, and take questions and have discussions. I try to choose funny books that are on the short side with clear illustrations and no details that might get lost on a webcam. The discussions are the most interesting. When we read Two of Everything, I asked second graders what they would like two of. Answers included “my mom,” “Zeke” (the teacher’s toddler), “PS5” (a really expensive video game console), and “999 Lions.” After some talk of odd and even numbers, the lions were revised slightly down to 998. I learned that one student used to be scared of chickens because their grandma’s chicken pecked them “and nobody saved me because my auntie was filming.” And everyone wants to be able to talk to dogs. When I show them my online virtual reading room, I highlight new books that have arrived at the library during the pandemic. They get to vote on a book to look up in the library catalog. Dog Man won in a recent week. I’ve checked with colleagues and learned this is a citywide phenomenon: the winner is invariably Dog Man. After we talk about how to request Dog Man for sidewalk pickup, it’s time for questions. These are usually, but not always, about the library. My favorite was when the discussion veered off into personal questions and ended up with my guinea pigs meeting a student’s guinea pigs. All the guinea pigs sniffed the screen, no doubt wondering if it was edible. Seeing the students’ faces is truly the highlight of my week, and I can’t wait to see all of you in person again. HOURS & LOCATION Piedmont Avenue Branch Library is located at 80 Echo Avenue in back of Piedmont Avenue Elementary School. For more information, call 510-597-5011 or see the website: https://oaklandlibrary.org/locations/piedmont-avenue-branch. Hours of operation are 10 a.m. to 1 p.m. Tuesday through Saturday. Closed Sunday and Monday. Margaret Rodriguez was the Piedmont Ave. Branch children’s librarian for many years and is now the Children’s Librarian at the Asian Branch. It’s possible to turn away from fear by gaining a clearer view of God as Love itself, which can have a tangible, healing effect in your life and in the world. articles.text: Molly Cliff Hilts, a Piedmont High Graduate in 1976, passed away on January 21, 2021 in Portland, Oregon after suffering with cancer for 18 months. She died peacefully at home, surrounded by love. She was 62, Born Molly Cliff on February 20, 1958 in Palo Alto, she was the oldest of four children of Lee and Nell Cliff. She graduated from Piedmont High School in 1976 and attended the University of Oregon. She graduated from Porter College at the University of California at Santa Cruz with a BA in Studio Arts. She met her husband Dave in 1977 while attending the University of Oregon. They reconnected in 1988 and were married in 1991. Dave was Molly’s rock, a loving and patient husband, multi-talented and solid. Molly’s interests and activities were diverse, especially her passion as an artist, community organizer, fundraiser, and volunteer. Her friends were many and spanned the breadth of her life. She received many honors and awards for her support of the arts and education. Molly was a member of the Portland Art Museum Education Committee, the Resource Council for LiveWire! radio theater, and was co-founder of the Portland Brooklyn Project. While Molly was with LiveWire!, she organized a show in Pendleton, Oregon, aired on Oregon Public Broadcasting. A dynamic social alchemist, Molly was known for her salons, a practice that began in 2000 in her beautiful historic home. Gatherings with food, libation, and art, the salons evolved over the years to include artists from other disciplines: musicians, poets, writers. It was a tradition dating back to 1911, when her great-grandmother and great-grandfather, Mary Porter Sesnon, and William T. Sesnon, first hosted similar salons that melded music, theatre, art, and the spoken word at their summer home, “Pino Alto” in Santa Cruz. In 2018, Molly created an exhibition of her artwork, as well as an endowment at the Mary Porter Sesnon Gallery at UC Santa Cruz’s Porter College in California. When Molly first moved to Portland in 1990, she unwittingly had a local grunge rock band pluck her name from the phone book as the name of their band. Flyers were posted all over town. The band, “Molly Cliff”, had quite a following for a time. Molly was an extraordinary painter and printmaker. She recently was captivated by illustrating crows and ravens, who frequently gathered in the trees outside of her studio in the attic. Artist Molly Cliff Hilts, who graduated from Piedmont High school in 1976, passed away on January 21. She was 62. Her gallery exhibiting her paintings stands at the edge of their garden. Her work can be viewed online at https://www.mollycliffhilts.com/#1, or through March 7 at the Brumfield Gallery in Astoria, Oregon (https://www.brumfieldgallery.com/molly-cliff-hilts. html). Her story, art, and a video interview can be seen at The Art of Connection: Interview with Portland Artist Molly Cliff Hilts | Rental Sales Gallery. Her paintings have been exhibited in solo shows in New York City, Oregon, California, Washington, and Mexico. She is represented by galleries in New York City, Philadelphia, North Carolina, and Oregon. Her work can be found in notable collections worldwide, including the private collection of Bill and Melinda Gates. Two weeks prior to Molly’s passing, she discovered that her painting titled “Eagle Creek” was placed in the Portland Museum of Art’s permanent collection of Northwest Art where it will live forever, a well-deserved recognition of her talents. A born artist, Molly wore her passion on her sleeve. If nothing appeared to be happening, she would make something happen. She had an inner drive that was powered by an innate desire to create.
