She died peacefully at home, surrounded by love. She was 62, Born Molly Cliff on February 20, 1958 in Palo Alto, she was the oldest of four children of Lee and Nell Cliff. She graduated from Piedmont High School in 1976 and attended the University of Oregon. She graduated from Porter College at the University of California at Santa Cruz with a BA in Studio Arts. She met her husband Dave in 1977 while attending the University of Oregon. They reconnected in 1988 and were married in 1991. Dave was Molly’s rock, a loving and patient husband, multi-talented and solid. Molly’s interests and activities were diverse, especially her passion as an artist, community organizer, fundraiser, and volunteer. Her friends were many and spanned the breadth of her life. She received many honors and awards for her support of the arts and education. For those of us in the Bay Area and beyond, who have wanted the vaccine from the beginning, the distribution efforts have been painfully slow. Dear MacMama: My MacBook Pro is 8 years old and running very slowly. I can’t open many web pages on Safari, it seems to take forever to start up. So, I am thinking about having the innards refreshed. I like the fact that I can play a CD or DVD from my large music collection in this laptop, and I know the newer ones don’t have that option. I called a local repair place and they can put in a Solid State Drive and more RAM for around $550. The laptop was originally a bit more than $1800, and I looked at the new version, and it would be about $2300 to get the specs that I want. The repairman told me that the new hard drive would last me several more years. Is it worth it or should I just get a new one? –Henri C., Montclair Dear Henri: Many times I get calls from customers asking me to help “clean up” or “speed up” an older Mac. Sometimes we can clean up and speed up a sluggish machine, but in many cases the computer is just too old. Let’s look at the possibilities. I have heard many stories of repair pros recommending upgrading older machines for a similar price tag; around $500. If you have the hard drive and RAM upgraded you will indeed have these new components that will likely last for years. But you will still have an 8-year-old screen, logic board and processor. And these will give out sooner than the new parts you have installed. So, it is likely that you will have partially robust insides, but the important components, like the logic board and processor will give out within a year or so. You should also note, you will still not be able to run the latest operating system (Big Sur). According to Apple, if certain conditions are met (your Mac has to be running Mojave to upgrade), Catalina (OS 10.15) is compatible. Since Catalina breaks the compatibility of older 32 bit software, many folks with older Macs find that the applications they depend on won’t run. And the success of running Catalina on an 8-year-old computer is spotty at best. And I feel your pain regarding the ability to play your CDs. I know many of us are still grumbling (including my husband) about Apple’s decision get rid of the internal optical drive. Apple did this to reduce weight and to promote the ever-expanding market of digital music. Since many music lovers are now moving to the mp3 download marketplace, CDs and vinyl recordings are becoming a thing of the past. But musicians (like me) still make CDs and some even are still recording to vinyl, since analog recordings are warmer than digital tracks. Newer models (as of 2013) do not have optical drives but you can purchase an external DVD/CD player that can attach to a new Mac. Apple’s USB Super Drive is around $80, and attaches via USB A, which means you will need a USB to USB-C adapter to use it on a new Mac. You can also share the CD/DVD drive of an older Mac across your network, but most of us want to be mobile with our laptops, so this is not always an option. So even though you can install these new components in your older laptop, in my opinion, it’s just wasted money. If you look at the life of your machine, you spend $1800 on your laptop and got 8 years of good service. That’s $225 a year. So. the idea of spending $500 to extend the life for maybe 1 more year does not make financial sense. And with the new M1 chip in the MacBook Air, now is a great time to buy a new laptop! For the elders in a family, social isolation can exacerbate feelings of loneliness, hopelessness, and despair, while the children lose the sense of being the recipient of the unique love of a grandparent. Seniors who are no longer working or actively engaged in their community, may find that the time they spend with their grandchildren is essential to their feelings of self-worth. Seniors wonder: What’s the point of staying healthy when I am separated from everyone I love? When does the risk associated with being in contact with my grandchildren become acceptable? Life can change in an instant; every moment away from my grandchildren is a loss. One approach to this dilemma is to evaluate the risk of contact. If all family members have been diligent in their safety practices, it may be that limited physical contact (outdoors, short visits, wearing facemasks) between the generations may constitute an acceptable risk that brings great rewards. Balancing risk and reward is a personal decision for every family. When that balance is reached, it may answer the question about whether or not, in your family, grandparents and grandchildren really need each other. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has lived in Piedmont for over 36 years. She is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides, counseling, support, and education for grandparents. articles.text: Oakland Coliseum to open as vaccination site this week People age 65 years and older, in addition to emergency services workers and essential education workers are among a new group of people who began receiving COVID-19 vaccines in Alameda County on February 8. Phase 1B Tier 1 includes people age 65 years and older as well as essential workers in the food, agriculture, emergency services, education and childcare sectors. This entire group numbers approximately 325,000 residents according to the Alameda County Public Health Department. Eligible residents are encouraged to contact their healthcare provider or employer to receive a vaccination appointment. Alameda County waited a few weeks and continued to focus on Phase 1A before opening up eligibility to Phase 1B Tier 1. The state allowed counties to begin vaccinating the latter phase on January 26. articles.text: As our lives were transformed in the spring of 2020 as a result of the global pandemic, people turned to…baking bread. Yes, and this wasn’t the only pastime to surge in popularity as more time was being spent at home. Let’s take a look at the hobbies and activities that people have discovered or returned to as they adjusted to a new normal. While the hoarding and resulting shortage of toilet paper made headlines, another staple was disappearing from grocery store shelves: flour. In May, The Atlantic reported that one company saw baking flour sales increase 2,000%. On social media, people were sharing photos of their fresh baked goods and sourdough starters, while manufacturers and wheat producers had difficulties meeting demand. Presumably no one set out to grow their own wheat just to bake a few loaves of bread, but people did decide this was an ideal time to grow some of their own food; either out of fear about the stability of our food supply or finally having time to tend a vegetable garden. The Burpee Seed Company reported that they sold more seed in March 2020 than any time in its 144-year history. The interest was worldwide, not just in the United States, as would-be gardeners needed to learn how to start seedlings and manage their tracts of land. Some seed companies had to stop taking orders during this influx just to meet demand. Perhaps a few of the new gardeners will be practicing songs, as another surprise trend was a significant increase in orders of musical instruments, including grand pianos, according to an article in The New York Times. The demand seemed to come from families with children who needed something to do or could no longer go to their lessons in person, but also from throngs of people seeking out a form of relief in playing instruments. Other changes in behavior reported in the news over the last year have included a dramatic increase in hiking and camping, reading more books, and more person-to-person letter writing. By Cynthia Kane Part 3 in a series If you grew up in a family where your grandparents were deceased, very elderly, or lived far away, you might conclude that grandparents are non-essential contributors to a child’s overall growth and development. After all, you didn’t have grandparents, and you turned out just fine. On the other hand, if your grandmother and/or grandfather played an important role in your everyday family life, you might have the opinion that Yes, children need grandparents! You can cite numerous examples of how your life was influenced for the better by the contact you had with a grandparent; the unconditional love you felt from them, the life lessons you learned, and the family lore that was passed down to you by your elders. Studies seem to show that families and cultures that place high value on interdependence, the sharing of family tasks (including childcare), and a give-andtake relationship between young and old, demonstrate increased closeness between grandparents and grandchildren. Families that instead value independence and individuality often find that the grandparent-grandchild bond may be less strong. The COVID-19 pandemic has meant that many grandparents and grandchildren have been separated from each other for nearly a year. Once most of us are vaccinated, this will surely change. But until then, seniors, especially those with comorbid conditions, have been advised to stay away from loved ones they don’t live with to reduce the risk of contracting COVID-19. For both young and old, this separation can be devastating. For the elders in a family, social isolation can exacerbate feelings of loneliness, hopelessness, and despair, while the children lose the sense of being the recipient of the unique love of a grandparent. Seniors who are no longer working or actively engaged in their community, may find that the time they spend with their grandchildren is essential to their feelings of self-worth. Seniors wonder: What’s the point of staying healthy when I am separated from everyone I love? When does the risk associated with being in contact with my grandchildren become acceptable? Life can change in an instant; every moment away from my grandchildren is a loss. One approach to this dilemma is to evaluate the risk of contact. If all family members have been diligent in their safety practices, it may be that limited physical contact (outdoors, short visits, wearing facemasks) between the generations may constitute an acceptable risk that brings great rewards. Balancing risk and reward is a personal decision for every family. When that balance is reached, it may answer the question about whether or not, in your family, grandparents and grandchildren really need each other. articles.text: Ah, good old Piedmont. If they can make a poor decision, they will do it every time. I have lived in our house most of my life – since I was nine years old. My father had the house built. The amount of drama that has unfolded during all those years is amazing. I have heard in recent years that the school population has gone down because young families were not eagerly signing up for a house that cost millions. And so, the choice was made to allow children who had grandparents living in Piedmont to attend Piedmont schools, because the overall school population was getting smaller. As example, our class, PHS ‘64, was large, with 205 kids. I think that the decision to let grandchildren attend Piedmont schools is a good one. There have been children of City employees attending Piedmont schools as long as I can remember, and that diversity never upset the carefully crafted Piedmont applecart. One of the reasons that the school population has diminished is because not all the children who live in our city choose to go to Piedmont schools. Perhaps, the School Board and teachers should be asking themselves that question. Many parents and children choose a different route. Why? Piedmont schools are not a one-size-fits-all model. Let the grandchildren into the schools. The system will be better for that decision. They will bring a more diverse group, and a sense of Piedmont history with them (especially if the grandparents have lived here as long as we have). This is not rocket science; it is being inclusive and welcoming to children rather than exclusive. Children should not be made to feel unwelcome. It is our job as caring adults to give them a wonderful childhood. Welcome them now. Terry Sarver is a Piedmont High graduate, Class of 1964, and a resident for 65 years.
